ImageDescription.value: The Tepees in Petrified Forest National Park in northeastern Arizona, United States. View is toward the northwest from the main park road. According to a National Park Service (NPS) document, rock strata exposed in the Tepees area of the park belong to the Blue Mesa Member of the Chinle Formation and are about 220 to 225 million years old. The colorful bands of mudstone and sandstone were laid down during the Triassic, when the area was part of a huge tropical floodplain.

ImageDescription.value:
Worm Bay at Port Campbell National Park, Peterborough, Victoria, Australia
Port Campbell National Park is located on the south coast of Victoria along the Great Ocean Road and protects a spectacular coastal landscape of limestone, cliffs, caves, and natural bridges.
Its geological formation dates back millions of years: over thousands of years, layers of limestone and shells formed caves, gateways, and towers, which were repeatedly eroded by the Southern Ocean. The coast also served as a habitat for indigenous groups in the region, including the Wergaia and Eastern Maar communities. From the 1950s/60s onwards, the area was designated a protected area to preserve its exceptional geology, wildlife, and flora and to manage visitor flows in a sensible manner.
Special features include the famous limestone cliffs, narrow passages, natural bridges, and steep cliffs; highlights such as the Twelve Apostles, Loch Ard Gorge, and other coastal formations attract many visitors each year. The sea is home to seals, seabirds, and rich marine fauna, while the rocky shores also support maritime flora. Hiking trails, lookout points, and boat tours offer insights into geology, geomorphology, and coastal protection—a harmonious combination of natural wonders and historical perspective.

ImageDescription.value:
Three Sisters, Blue Mountains National Park, New South Wales, Australia
The Blue Mountains National Park is located west of Sydney and is one of Australia’s most famous natural areas. Its history is closely linked to Aboriginal culture, particularly that of the Gundungurra and Darug peoples, who have inhabited the area for tens of thousands of years and have a spiritual connection to the landscape.
For European settlers, the rugged sandstone plateaus were long considered an insurmountable obstacle. It was not until 1813 that Gregory Blaxland, William Lawson, and William Charles Wentworth succeeded in crossing the mountains, opening the way for the development of the Australian hinterland.
In the 19th century, parts of the region were used for logging and mining, while at the same time its scenic appeal was discovered. In 1959, the Blue Mountains National Park was officially established to protect the unique eucalyptus vegetation, deep gorges, and waterfalls.
In 2000, UNESCO declared the area part of the Greater Blue Mountains Area a World Heritage Site. Today, the park stands for nature conservation, tourism, and recognition of Australia’s indigenous cultural history.

Beauchamp Falls in Great Otway National Park, Beech Forest, Victoria, Australia
Efforts to protect Great Otway National Park began in the early 1900s, when the first areas of lush rainforest and coastal landscapes were placed under protection.
In 1967, the park was officially established as Great Otway National Park to preserve its diverse ecosystems, including dense eucalyptus forests, waterfalls, and coastal areas. In the following decades, the park’s area was significantly expanded through the merger of several protected areas.
The park is also significant to Aboriginal culture, whose people have lived in the region for thousands of years and whose traditions and connection to the land are honored and protected within the park.

ImageDescription.value:
Canoes on the coast, Tsitsikamma National Park, Eastern Cape, South Africa
Tsitsikamma National Park is located on the famous Garden Route in the Eastern Cape province. It was established in 1964 and was one of Africa’s first marine national parks. Today, it is part of the larger Garden Route National Park.
The name “Tsitsikamma” comes from the Khoikhoi language and means “place with plenty of water”. The park protects an impressive coastal landscape with steep cliffs, dense evergreen forests, and a species-rich marine area.
The suspension bridges at the mouth of the Storms River are famous for their spectacular views of the Indian Ocean. In addition to coastal and marine conservation, the park also includes parts of the original Afro-montane forest with large yellowwood trees.
